drills.label: Cold open
drills.question_line: SAM: Here's your item. A company runs an internal H R assistant built on the Agent S D K. Employees ask
drills.answer_line: SAM: C is right. Identity comes from the server, and the tool enforces
drills.stem: An internal HR assistant on the Agent SDK calls an HR database tool via one service account that reads every employee record. The system prompt says: return only the requester's records, plus direct reports if the user says they are a manager. Which change best closes the security gap?

options.A: Add few-shot examples showing the assistant refusing requests for other people's records
options.B: Add an output classifier that blocks any response containing another employee's name
options.C: Verify identity and role server-side from SSO; the tool returns only records that identity is entitled to
options.D: Log every call to the HR tool and review the logs weekly for misuse

drills.why: Identity comes from the server and the tool enforces authorization with it, so it cannot return a record the user isn't entitled to, whatever the model is persuaded to do.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Choose two. A field-service company gives its technicians an agent
drills.answer_line: SAM: A and C. A removes capabilities the role never needs
drills.scenario: Technician agent with leftover pilot tools
drills.stem: Technicians' agent looks up work orders, checks parts stock and searches manuals. Pilot config also has a tool running arbitrary SQL on the warehouse and a customer-credit tool. A manual-search subagent shares the orchestrator's full tool set. Which two changes best reduce risk?

options.A: Remove the SQL and credit tools, and record why each was removed
options.B: Add a system prompt instruction telling the agent never to issue credits
options.C: Restrict the manual-search subagent to read-only search tools
options.D: Route every credit through a supervisor confirmation screen
options.E: Log all warehouse queries to the security team

drills.why: A removes capabilities the role never needs, killing the risk at the root. C scopes the subagent to its job. B, D and E leave the tools in place.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. A retail bank routes customer complaints to the right team
drills.answer_line: SAM: B. Necessity filter, reference identifier for routing
drills.stem: A retail bank uses Claude to summarize complaint text and pick a category. The server sends the complaint plus the full customer record: card number, date of birth, home address, account number. Which change best addresses the data-handling risk?

options.A: No change, because the API does not retain conversation content by default
options.B: Send only the complaint text and a complaint reference ID; strip other fields on the server before the call
options.C: Encrypt the application's request logs at rest
options.D: Truncate each request to its first 500 tokens to limit exposure

drills.why: Necessity filter: a reference ID is enough for routing, and redaction happens before the call. A ignores your own application's logs; C leaves card numbers in them.

drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Three quick ones: name the mechanism.
drills.prompt: Name the mechanism: a service for 3 Claude clients; 2 tools used by 1 product only; a procurement agent needing another team's risk agent.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Choose two. A public-sector benefits agent has all forty casework
drills.answer_line: SAM: A and C. Both stage context so each step carries what it needs
drills.stem: A public-sector benefits agent has all 40 casework procedures in its system prompt, plus definitions for 30 tools, on every call. Most cases use 2 or 3 procedures. Tool selection accuracy is slipping and per-call cost keeps rising. Which two changes best address this?

options.A: Package each procedure as a Skill, so only its description loads until a case needs it
options.B: Move to a model with a larger context window
options.C: Defer tool definitions until needed, keeping a small stable prefix that can be cached
options.D: Cut each procedure to its first paragraph to save tokens
options.E: Fine-tune a model on all 40 procedures

drills.why: Both stage context so each step carries what it needs, and the small stable prefix still gets the caching benefit. A bigger window is a ceiling, not a target.

drills.question_line: SAM: Before the tease, a test. Pause and name the four task statements this episode covered
drills.prompt: Name the four task statements this episode covered, and the giveaway for each.

In this episode: Spotting capability bloat: remove or gate a tool
Where identity and authorization must be enforced
Filtering what enters a Claude call by necessity
MCP vs direct API tool use vs agent-to-agent
Deferred discovery is not least privilege

5 layers: compliance, identity, authorization, data handling, observability
Capability bloat: every tool is an attack surface and a cost
Scope each subagent's tools to its task
Not needed: remove it; needed but high-stakes: gate it
Authentication and authorization: Identity verified on the server, never claimed in the user turn
Authorization deterministic and in code, before side-effecting calls
A broad service account is a path around the access policy
Multi-tenant: isolate with Workspaces, not a shared API key
The context window is not a data-governance boundary
Necessity, not convenience, decides what goes in
Connection mechanisms: Entry points, build-time interfaces, delivery routes
MCP and API tool use are different layers, not rivals
The deciding question is reuse across clients
Agent SDK for a multi-turn loop in your own product
Agent-to-agent: delegate an outcome, don't reach past the interface
Progressive discovery: Monolithic: bounded, stable, cacheable, needs everything at once
Progressive: load only what the next step needs
Skills load name and description first, full instructions on demand
Tool definitions can be deferred too
Deferring a tool doesn't remove the permission
Skills are bundled code: audit, sandbox, vetted registry
Cold open: the verdict: Answer: C, server-verified identity enforced by the tool itself
The tool can't return records the user isn't entitled to
B: a compensating control at the wrong layer
A: the model enforcing authorization, role read from the user turn
D: weekly log review finds a leak a week late
Five to remember: Remove, don't watch: drop tools the role doesn't need and record why
Identity from the server; authorization deterministic, in code at the tool and retrieval layer
The context window is not a governance boundary: necessity, a reference ID, redact before the call
MCP for several clients, direct API for one product, Agent SDK for loops, agent-to-agent to delegate
Progressive by default; monolithic for bounded, stable content; discovery decides when, not whether
Recap: the exam tells: Role never uses a tool → remove it, record why; role needs a dangerous tool → keep it, gate it
User message claims a role, like "as a manager" → unverified; identity comes from the server
Tools on one broad service account → authorization bypass, fixed in code at tool and retrieval
"Vendor doesn't retain content" → your logs still do; unneeded field → reference ID, redact first
Same tools for several clients → MCP; one product → direct API; another team's agent → agent-to-agent
Claude Code as a product backend → wrong
Every procedure and tool definition in every call, selection slipping → Skills and deferred tools
An option claims deferring a tool removes the risk → discovery decides when it loads, not whether
